Device Console and SSH Console

Run FortiOS CLI commands on an appliance over SSH, test a username and password against a device, and package the session for Fortinet TAC — plus the read-only SSH Console on each appliance page.

👤 ForOperatorAdministrator
🔑 Permissionsappliances.view appliances.apply users.manage
📍 WhereAdministrator → Device Console (administrators) or Automation → Device Console (other users with an edit permission), in every ADOM (URL /console/); per appliance: Appliances → <appliance> → Console (URL /appliances/<id>/console)

What is it?#

SATOM has two consoles that open an SSH session to an appliance:

  • The Device Console (Administrator or Automation → Device Console) is the one place in SATOM where SSH can change an appliance. You paste a script of CLI commands, SATOM runs it in one session and shows the answer to every line. The same page can test a single username and password against a FortiOS device, and build a redacted support bundle for a Fortinet TAC ticket.
  • The SSH Console on an appliance's page (Console button) is read-only: it accepts only get, show and diagnose commands, one at a time, and refuses a diagnose command that changes the device.

This article covers both. The node-side satom command-line tool (run on the SATOM server itself) is a different thing — see CLI.

What does it do?#

Device Console (/console/)

  • Runs up to 200 commands, one per line, in one SSH session, so config / edit / end blocks work as they do on the box.
  • Classifies every line before anything is sent:
  • forbidden — execute factoryreset, execute formatlogdisk, execute erase-disk, disk/USB-disk format. Refused at every permission level.
  • disruptive — execute reboot, execute shutdown, execute restore, execute ha …, execute backup|migrate … tftp|ftp, set password / set passwd (and unset of them). Sent only after you tick the acknowledgement and type the appliance name.
  • safe — everything else.
  • Reads abbreviations as the full command, the way the Fortinet CLI does: every keyword matches any prefix of itself, from one letter. exe reb asks for the same acknowledgement as execute reboot, set passw is a password change, and exe fa is refused like execute factoryreset. A keyword is a whole token, so exe hardware is not read as exe ha. A quoted single word counts as a keyword (execute "reboot"), and a line is also read with every ? removed, because ? is a help key on most Fortinet CLIs (exe reb?oot runs as exe reboot).
  • Gates the whole script before the session opens: one forbidden line means nothing is sent.
  • Stops at the first failed command by default and marks the rest not_run.
  • Reads each answer for FortiOS error markers (Command fail, a negative Return code, Unknown action, parse errors, permission denied, is invalid, entry not found, The object is in use). An empty answer counts as success.
  • Redacts secrets from the transcript (values after set of a password, passphrase, secret, PSK or key attribute — abbreviated, such as set passw …, or compound, such as auth-pwd, bind-password, psksecret-remote or md5-key — and PEM private keys) — they become «redacted by SATOM».
  • Test a credential — checks one username/password against any FortiOS host over SSH and reports reachable, authenticated and can read separately.
  • Send to Fortinet TAC — builds a .tar.gz with the redacted transcript and, optionally, the read-only diagnostic battery of the appliance's product (FortiWeb: 32 get/diagnose commands; FortiADC: its own battery; FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator: none).

SSH Console on an appliance (/appliances/<id>/console)

  • One command at a time; only the verbs get, show, diagnose and diag are accepted. Anything else is refused before SATOM connects.
  • A diagnose command is refused when one of its words changes the device: kill, clear, reset, delete, failover, sysrq/crash, set, enable/disable, format, fsck, rmmod and similar. Abbreviations count, because the CLI completes them: diag sys kil 11 1 reads as kill.
  • A list of read-only Presets (FortiWeb or FortiADC set, depending on the appliance kind). Clicking a preset runs it. Users who may not run commands see the presets and their commands as a read-only list.

Requirements#

  • The appliance is registered in Appliances with an SSH port (default 22) and the admin credential SATOM uses. SATOM reuses that credential for SSH.
  • The SSH Console on an appliance page is offered for FortiWeb and FortiADC appliances only. Other kinds get the flash "This action is not available for this appliance kind."
  • On a multi-ADOM FortiWeb registered as several rows, the SSH Console belongs to the chassis' device row (see The two consoles compared).

Permissions#

Action Required permission
Open the Device Console, Run, Build bundle the legacy config_write gate. Any one of these granular keys grants it: appliances.apply, appliances.edit, protection.edit, protection.apply, network.edit, network.apply, operations.apply, operations.template_save, operations.template_apply, operations.template_approve
Test login (credential test) users.manage
Open the SSH Console on an appliance appliances.view
Run in the SSH Console on an appliance appliances.apply
  • Without config_write, /console/ answers 403. The Device Console menu entry is drawn only for users with config_write: administrators find it in the Administrator group, every other such user (for example an Operator) in the Automation group.
  • Without users.manage, the Test a credential card shows: "Credential testing needs the user_manage permission — it accepts an arbitrary host, so it is the one control here that can be aimed at a device SATOM does not manage."
  • A Viewer can open the SSH Console on an appliance by URL (it needs only appliances.view). Without appliances.apply the page shows the presets as a read-only list and the notice "You can see this appliance and its preset commands, but running a command (even a read-only one) needs the "Run appliance actions" permission."; there is no Run box. The Console button on the appliance page and the terminal icon on the Appliances list are only shown with appliances.apply.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: operators now find the Device Console under Automation; the SSH Console hides Run from users who cannot run commands; and the Device Console presets and the TAC diagnostic battery follow the appliance's product instead of always sending FortiWeb commands.

ℹ️Note

Changed on 2026-10-14: abbreviations are classified like the full command from the first letter. Before, a prefix needed four letters, so exe fa was sent as an ordinary line and exe reb needed no acknowledgement. Transcripts and TAC bundles also redact abbreviated and compound secret attributes.

How to use#

Run commands in the Device Console#

  1. Open Administrator → Device Console (administrators) or Automation → Device Console (other users).
  2. In Appliance, pick a device (— pick one —). The list shows the appliances of the active ADOM; in the Global ADOM it shows every product.
  3. Type or paste the script in Commands — one per line, up to 200. Lines starting with # are comments.
  4. Optional: use Insert a read-only preset to append a preset command to the script. Only the presets of the picked appliance's product are offered (FortiWeb or FortiADC); FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator have none.
  5. Leave Stop at the first failed command ticked (recommended).
  6. Only if the script contains a disruptive command: tick I understand this script is disruptive and type the appliance name in the box below it (type the appliance name to confirm).
  7. Press Run.
  8. Read the Result column: one card per command with its tier (if not safe), its status (ok, error, refused, not_run) and the output. The header shows the number of commands and how many failed.

⚠️Warning — This console can change the appliance

The delete guard that protects shared objects in the web UI does not apply here: a CLI delete inside a config block can remove an object another policy still references. Check references before you delete from the CLI.

Build a TAC bundle#

  1. Run a script (the bundle form appears under the result once a transcript exists).
  2. In Send to Fortinet TAC, optionally enter the TAC ticket number (optional) and What you were trying to do (optional).
  3. Keep Attach the read-only diagnostic battery ticked to add the product's diagnostic commands (SATOM opens a second session for them). For a FortiAnalyzer or FortiAuthenticator SATOM has no battery; the bundle then holds the transcript and a DIAGNOSTICS-MISSING.txt saying so.
  4. Press Build bundle. The browser downloads tac-<appliance>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>.tar.gz (UTC time stamp).

Test a credential#

  1. In Test a credential, enter Host or IP, SSH port (default 22), Username and Password.
  2. Press Test login.
  3. Read the badges: reachable / unreachable, authenticated / not authenticated, can read / read not confirmed, and the time taken. If the login worked, the firmware (Firmware) and Device hostname from get system status are shown.
  4. Write-access hint (raw) shows what the box answered when the session tried to set the CLI pager. It is evidence, not a verdict: a box that refused it for another reason looks the same as a read-only account.

The device does not need to be registered in SATOM. The password is never stored and never shown in the result.

Use the read-only SSH Console on an appliance#

  1. Open Appliances, then the appliance. In Appliance Actions, press Console (on the Appliances list, the terminal icon does the same for FortiWeb and FortiADC rows). Both are shown only with appliances.apply.
  2. Click a preset in Presets, or type a command after $ and press Run (or Enter).
  3. The output appears below. Errors are shown as ERROR: <reason>.

The two consoles compared#

Device Console SSH Console (appliance page)
URL /console/ /appliances/<id>/console
Menu Administrator or Automation → Device Console (every ADOM) Console button on the appliance page
Writes to the device Yes — safe and (confirmed) disruptive commands No — get, show, diagnose, diag only
Input A script, up to 200 lines, one session One command per run
Open the page config_write appliances.view
Run config_write appliances.apply
Appliance kinds Any appliance visible in the active ADOM FortiWeb and FortiADC
Multi-ADOM chassis Every ADOM row is listed Only the chassis' device row; an ADOM row is redirected to it
Presets FortiWeb or FortiADC presets, matching the picked appliance FortiWeb presets, or FortiADC presets for a FortiADC
Extras Credential test, TAC bundle —
Audit action console.run, console.verify_credentials, console.tac_bundle appliance.console

Why the SSH Console is chassis-scoped. A FortiWeb in ADOM mode is registered as one row per ADOM, but the CLI acts on the whole box. When you open the console from an ADOM row, SATOM redirects you to the row that owns the device and flashes "Firmware, the backup vault and the console act on the whole appliance, not on — they live on ." If that row is not visible to you, you land on the Appliances list with "… The row that carries them is not visible to you."

Field Description Required Example
Host or IP Any FortiOS host Yes 192.0.2.20
SSH port 1–65535 No (22) 22
Username Account to test Yes admin

FortiWeb presets (both consoles): System status, Performance, HA status, Update info, Hardware (VM), CPU, Memory, Disk health, NIC list, Routing table, ARP list. FortiADC presets (both consoles): System status, Performance, HA status, Interfaces, Routing table, Netlink interfaces, Disk usage.

Example#

🧪Example — Change the DNS server on one appliance

Script in the Device Console, appliance fweb-01:

# point the box at the new resolver
config system dns
  set primary 192.0.2.53
end
get system dns

All four lines are safe, so no acknowledgement is needed. The three configuration lines return no output (no output — normal for a configuration command that succeeded); get system dns shows the new value. If config system dns had failed, the script would stop there and the set line would be marked not_run instead of landing at the top level of the CLI.

Result#

  • Each Run and Test login, each Build bundle, and each SSH Console command that completes is written to the Audit log. console.run records the appliance, the commands (redacted), their tiers, whether a disruptive acknowledgement was given, the stop-on-error setting and the failure count. console.verify_credentials records host, username and port, the three results and any error — never the password.
  • Run, Test login and SSH Console commands are device actions: one that takes longer than the inline window (about two seconds by default) continues as a background job in the Jobs dock. Build bundle is not a job; it streams the download.
  • A TAC bundle contains meta.json (appliance, kind, firmware, ticket, note, time stamp, redacted: true), console-session.txt (the redacted transcript) and either diagnostics.txt or, when the battery could not be captured, DIAGNOSTICS-MISSING.txt explaining why. A copy is kept in the SATOM data directory.

Troubleshooting#

"Pick an appliance first."#

Possible causes - Run was pressed with — pick one — still selected.

Solution 1. Choose an appliance in Appliance and press Run again.

Verification - The Result column shows one card per command.

"No commands were entered."#

Possible causes - The script is empty or contains only # comment lines.

Solution 1. Enter at least one command that does not start with #.

Verification - The result header shows 1 cmd or more.

"This script contains a disruptive command. Tick the acknowledgement and type the appliance name exactly (…) to send it."#

Possible causes - The script contains a reboot, shutdown, restore, HA, clear-text backup/migrate or password command — written in full or abbreviated (exe reb, set passw) — and the checkbox is not ticked or the typed name differs from the appliance name (it is compared exactly). The disruptive row itself reads refused: … Tick 'I understand this script is disruptive' and type the appliance name to send it.

Solution 1. Tick I understand this script is disruptive. 2. Type the appliance name exactly as shown in the flash message. 3. Press Run again.

Verification - The rows show ok/error instead of not_run, and the disruptive lines carry the disruptive badge.

"refused: … This command has no path through SATOM at any permission level"#

Possible causes - A line matched the forbidden tier (factory reset, format log disk, erase disk, disk format). The match is made anywhere in the unquoted part of the line, so a line pasted from a session log such as FortiWeb # execute factoryreset is still recognised. - The line is an abbreviation of a forbidden command: exe fa, exe factoryres or exec format are read exactly like the full words, because the device CLI runs them that way.

Solution 1. Remove the line. If you really need it, run it from the appliance's own console. 2. A value that merely mentions such a command must be quoted with its spaces (FortiOS requires quotes around values with spaces); a quoted span that contains whitespace is not scanned. A quoted single word is scanned as a keyword.

Verification - Nothing was sent: every other row shows not sent — the script was refused before it ran.

All rows show "the session never opened"#

Possible causes - The appliance is unreachable on its SSH port, the stored credential is wrong, or the stored host key does not match.

Solution 1. Use Test a credential with the same host and port to tell unreachable apart from not authenticated. 2. Correct the host, SSH port or credential on the appliance in Appliances.

Verification - Test login shows reachable and authenticated, and a new Run returns output.

"… the appliance host is a retired placeholder (…), so nothing was sent"#

Possible causes - The appliance's host ends in .invalid (marked · retired in the picker). SATOM does not dial it.

Solution 1. Pick the live appliance, or update the host in Appliances if the device is back in service.

Verification - The picker entry no longer shows · retired.

"12 credential checks in 300s is the limit for one operator — try again in …s."#

Possible causes - More than 12 credential tests by the same user within 5 minutes.

Solution 1. Wait the number of seconds shown and test again. The tool tests one credential you already have; it is not meant to search for one.

Verification - Test login returns badges instead of the error.

"the credential was accepted but 'get system status' returned nothing usable …"#

Possible causes - The account logs in but its admin profile has no read access.

Solution 1. Give the account an admin profile with read access on the device, then test again.

Verification - The can read badge turns green and Firmware is shown.

"'…' is not a read-only command — only diag, diagnose, get, show are allowed in the console"#

Possible causes - A command other than get/show/diagnose/diag was typed in the SSH Console on an appliance page. Each statement separated by ;, & or | is checked.

Solution 1. Use a read command, or use the Device Console if you need to change the device (requires config_write).

Verification - The output shows the command's answer instead of ERROR:.

"refused '…': '…' changes the device state"#

Possible causes - A diagnose command typed in the SSH Console contains a word that changes the device, for example diagnose debug kernel sysrq command crash or diagnose sys kill …. An abbreviation reads as the full word: the message then says 'kil' reads as 'kill', which changes the device state.

Solution 1. Use a read-only diagnose command. A command that must change the device belongs in the Device Console, with its acknowledgement gates.

Verification - The output shows the command's answer instead of ERROR:.

The SSH Console sends you to another appliance row#

Possible causes - You opened the console on an ADOM row of a multi-ADOM FortiWeb; the console belongs to the chassis' device row.

Solution 1. Use the device row named in the flash message.

Verification - The page title reads Console — .

Advanced#

Advanced Where the rules live

The tier rules, the error markers and the redaction live in one service shared by the Device Console page and the Console script step of the former Process section; the page only adds the typed confirmation. A Process step is stricter: a disruptive step must name the one appliance it may disrupt.

The read-only SSH Console uses a separate allowlist (get, show, diagnose, diag) that other read-only SSH features also rely on; the Device Console does not relax it. Since 2026-10-14 every diagnose statement must also pass the state-changing word rule; before that, any diagnose command was accepted. Diagnose Log Collection and the Diagnostic Battery apply a stricter version that also refuses commands that never return or send traffic.

Advanced Session details
  • Both consoles open an interactive shell, disable the CLI pager at the start of the session and pin the appliance's SSH host key on first contact; a later mismatch refuses the connection.
  • On the Device Console the pager change (config system console / set output standard / end) is the only write SATOM performs without being asked; its answer is the Write-access hint (raw) of the credential test and appears as # pager setup at the top of a transcript.
  • Scripts longer than 200 commands are cut; a note says how many were not sent.
  • The credential-test rate limit is kept in memory per SATOM process.
Advanced Limits worth knowing
  • SATOM has no presets and no diagnostic battery for FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator. On those, type the commands the device speaks.
  • The Device Console lists every ADOM row of a multi-ADOM chassis and is not chassis-scoped, unlike the SSH Console on the appliance page.
